The Swampfish Chologaster cornuta is a small, troglobitic-looking member of the family Amblyopsidae that nonetheless inhabits surface and subterranean waters of the Atlantic Coastal Plain. Field records indicate that individuals achieve a maximum standard length of 5.7 cm [Li = 5.7 cm] in natural populations, a size considerably smaller than that of its congener the northern cavefish Amblyopsis spelaea. A newly emerged yolk-sac larva exhibits a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.00052 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00052 grams], which is among the lowest recorded for any amblyopsid species. During the incubation period, embryonic development occurs at a stable 13 °C [T = 13 °C], leading to an age at birth of roughly 18 days [ab = roughly 18 days] following gamete fusion. This protracted yolk-dependent interval reflects the cold, food-poor conditions typical of its spring-fed habitats.

Reproductive activity in Chologaster cornuta unfolds at a notably sedate pace under the same thermal regime. Gravid females produce clutches containing one to two eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = one to two eggs per spawning event], and the inter-spawning interval is prolonged such that fewer than one clutch is completed per year [F_R_i = one clutch is completed per year]. The resulting daily reproduction rate, equivalent to approximately 0.27 offspring per year [Ri = approximately 0.27 offspring per year], reflects an energetic strategy adapted to oligotrophic environments. The onset of gonadal recrudescence is equally delayed; puberty is attained approximately 244 days after hatching [tp = approximately 244 days after hatching] when rearing temperatures are held at 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. This slow maturation contrasts with the rapid life cycles of most epigean cypriniforms and underscores the effect of a consistently cool thermal environment on reproductive physiology.

Body size at the onset of reproductive maturity is tightly correlated with standard length. Individuals first exhibit vitellogenesis or spermiation at a standard length of approximately 3.6 cm [Lp = approximately 3.6 cm], corresponding to roughly 63 percent of the ultimate adult size. The wet weight at puberty, estimated from morphometric relationships, is approximately 0.46 grams [Wwp = approximately 0.46 grams], a figure that aligns with the lean body composition typical of cave-adapted fishes. A fully grown, reproductively active adult achieves an ultimate wet weight of about 1.7 grams [Wwi = about 1.7 grams], the highest mass recorded in long-term captive colonies. This modest increment from pubertal to terminal mass indicates that most post-juvenile energy is allocated to maintenance and reproductive effort rather than continued somatic growth, a pattern common among amblyopsids inhabiting stable but resource-limited groundwater systems.

Longevity in the Swampfish, when assessed under controlled conditions at 13 °C [T = 13 °C], reaches 3650 days [am = 3650 days] for the oldest documented individuals, equivalent to a full decade. This considerable duration is remarkable for a fish of such diminutive size and likely arises from low metabolic demand and reduced predation pressure within its refugial habitat. The age at birth under these same conditions was confirmed at roughly 18 days [ab = roughly 18 days], a value derived from repeated laboratory observations at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. The juxtaposition of an 18-day embryonic period against a 244-day interval to pubertal maturation (244 days after hatching) [tp = 244 days after hatching] highlights a life-history strategy dominated by a prolonged juvenile phase at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. This extended pre-reproductive window allows gradual accumulation of sufficient lipid stores to support gamete production and spawning in an environment where food resources are seasonally unpredictable.

Comparative physiological analyses place the lifetime reproductive output of Chologaster cornuta among the lowest for any iteroparous teleost. Under the standard thermal regimen of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], a female produces fewer than one clutch per year [F_R_i = fewer than one clutch per year], with each event yielding no more than 2 eggs [N_R_i = each event yielding no more than 2 eggs], resulting in a maximum fecundity of roughly 10 to 12 eggs over a decade-long lifespan. The ultimate standard length of 5.7 cm [Li = 5.7 cm] is reached only after several years of slow growth, and the weight at puberty of 0.46 grams [Wwp = 0.46 grams] is not surpassed until the third or fourth year. This combination of late maturity, negligible fecundity, and extreme longevity represents a classic K-selected life-history syndrome that is exceptionally rare among freshwater fishes and likely reflects the stable but severely energy-limited character of the coastal plain aquifer systems this species occupies.
